profiles.title: Observer
profiles.canonical_definition: A participant in knowing whose distinctions, descriptions, and actions are themselves open to observation and question.
profiles.summary: In von Foerster's second-order cybernetics, an account of observing must include the activity of its observer. Ask what a description lets its user notice and do, and what the use of that description changes.
profiles.why_it_matters: A problem can be sustained by the way it is described. Changing the question may disclose an action that an established description has ruled out.
key_distinctions: observing a situation versus examining how it is being observed
a description's effects versus its author's intentions
acknowledging one's participation versus being authorised to represent others
historical_lineage: Von Foerster's cybernetics of observing systems; this profile uses the 2003 reprint of an earlier address and interview.
practice_connections: Keep one observation fixed and change the question asked of it. What becomes possible?
Ask what work a stated purpose is doing: which actions does it permit, excuse, or hide?
Name a person who could challenge this description, the evidence they could offer, and what would change if they were right.
common_misreadings: Self-reference makes every account equally adequate.
Including myself in an account proves that I have included everyone affected.
Von Foerster's ethical proposals are demonstrated laws of nature.
open_checks: The practice questions are editorial applications, not a prescribed von Foerster procedure.
Test observer claims against specific research practices; do not replace empirical checking with a declaration of reflexivity.

locators.claim: Observer participation and questions about the use of purpose are source exposition.

profiles.editorial_note: The definition and practice questions are editorial formulations informed by von Foerster. The comparison with representation and legitimacy is an editorial distinction, not a claim of equivalence with CSH. No new human approval is implied.

profiles.title: Multiple perspectives
profiles.canonical_definition: Inquiry into how a situation changes when participants' purposes, boundaries, evidence, and possibilities for action are described from different positions.
profiles.summary: Different accounts may expose a disagreement about what is happening, what matters, or whose action is possible. SSM uses declared worldviews and models to structure inquiry; CSH questions the facts and values made relevant by a boundary. These are distinct ways of working with differences.
profiles.why_it_matters: An inquiry needs to test alternative accounts and allow them to challenge its framing. That test may justify keeping the original question, changing a proposed action, or exposing a conflict that still requires a decision.
key_distinctions: different observations versus different criteria of improvement
comparing accounts versus merging them into one model
accommodation for action versus identical worldviews
opportunity to contribute versus authority to decide
historical_lineage: This entry compares Checkland's SSM and Ulrich's CSH without claiming either exhausts the idea or that one descends from the other.
practice_connections: Write two coherent accounts of the same proposed change, including what would count as success in each.
Keep a disagreement that changes the action visible. Record who must decide it and whose objection remains.
Test an alternative framing by naming an action it makes available and the evidence that would justify trying it.
common_misreadings: A larger list of views guarantees fairness or completeness.
Respect for people requires treating every factual claim as equally supported.
Agreement to a course of action means the participants now share one interpretation.
open_checks: The practice questions are editorial applications, not a combined SSM–CSH method.
Whether people can object safely, and whether an accommodation is legitimate, need evidence from the actual setting.

profiles.title: Boundary critique
profiles.canonical_definition: Critical examination of the judgements that make some facts, values, people, and consequences relevant to a claim while excluding or subordinating others.
profiles.summary: Ulrich's CSH examines motivation, power, knowledge, and legitimation. Comparing existing and proposed boundary judgements can expose whose version of improvement a claim serves; it does not compute the uniquely right boundary.
profiles.why_it_matters: A technically defensible proposal may leave the people bearing its costs unable to question its purpose. Examining that exclusion changes what the proposal can legitimately claim.
key_distinctions: validity within an account versus legitimacy of its use for action
people involved in deciding versus people affected by the decision
asking what is the case versus asking what ought to be the case
surfacing a judgement versus settling it
historical_lineage: Ulrich's Critical Systems Heuristics; the normative focus is explicit in his author primer and 2022 account.
practice_connections: Take one claimed improvement. Name its beneficiary, measure of success, decision-maker, and person bearing a consequence outside that measure.
Change one of those judgements and identify which evidence or recommendation changes with it.
Record how those affected can challenge the premises, and who has authority to act on that challenge.
common_misreadings: Boundary critique is a stakeholder list or a wider diagram.
Completing twelve questions establishes the right boundary.
People attending an inquiry thereby authorise its conclusions.
One fixed ordering of is and ought questions is compulsory.
open_checks: The practice questions are editorial applications, not a replacement twelve-question framework.
A route for legitimate decision and contest remains necessary; the questions alone do not establish it.

profiles.title: Structure and agency
profiles.canonical_definition: The relation between conditions of social action and the activities through which those conditions are reproduced or changed.
profiles.summary: In Bhaskar's transformational model, a round of action starts within social forms it did not create, while their continuation depends on activity. Reproduction and transformation are both possible; recognising their relation does not tell us which change a particular actor can achieve.
profiles.why_it_matters: Reframing a problem may change what people consider doing while leaving a contract, resource allocation, or authority relation in place. A proposal needs an account of how those conditions could actually change.
key_distinctions: conditions inherited before an action versus outcomes produced through it
acting intentionally versus intending every social consequence
imagining an alternative versus meeting the conditions of transition
historical_lineage: Bhaskar's later retrospective account of his transformational model; Challoner's researcher module remains a separate secondary reconstruction.
practice_connections: Name a condition that predates the current initiative and the activity that keeps it in force.
Specify which actors could change it, with what authority and resources, and through which sequence of actions.
Distinguish an account that has changed from a social relation that has changed; seek evidence for each.
common_misreadings: Structures exist wholly independently of human activity.
Because people reproduce structures, any individual can choose to remove them.
Bhaskar's TMSA, Giddens's structuration, and Archer's analytical dualism are interchangeable names.
An abstract ontology supplies a ready-made intervention.
open_checks: Giddens and Archer have not been independently source-checked in this pass. Bhaskar's own comparison cannot settle their differences.
The 1979 book itself has not been inspected here; the primary account is a 2011 presentation published in 2020.
Test the proposed mechanism and transition conditions in the setting; the general account does not establish them.

reader_prose.heading: What would have to change?
reader_prose.text:
A service team describes repeated contact as failure to follow instructions. A different account treats it as evidence that the route to help doesn't fit people's circumstances. Each description suggests different observations and actions. The team can ask what its first description has made hard to notice, and what evidence would change its judgement.

That is an original example of an observer question. Bringing in other accounts may change the team's understanding, but a meeting doesn't establish whose concerns should govern a decision. Ulrich's boundary critique asks about that judgement: who benefits, who controls the means of change, and who can challenge a claim made on their behalf? Making a boundary visible gives people something to question; it doesn't itself make the boundary legitimate.

Checkland's SSM offers models built from declared worldviews to structure inquiry and seek accommodations for action. Participants may act together while differences remain. Whether a particular accommodation is fair, or whether someone can refuse it without penalty, still needs examination. Neither a diagram nor agreement among those present settles that.

A further question concerns what must change outside the conversation. Bhaskar's account starts each round of action within inherited social conditions. If the team identifies a better route but cannot alter the contract, resources, or decision rights that sustain the present one, it needs a way to change those conditions. The account of the situation and the conditions of action can change at different rates. Evidence is needed for both.

These traditions can inform the same inquiry without becoming one theory. The example and practical connections are editorial applications; they don't establish that the authors share an ontology or that one method guarantees the next step.
reader_prose.basis: Original fictional service example and editorial comparison, with attributed source exposition. No private client case or empirical outcome is implied.
